title: Event-Time Order-Flow Memory, Operational-Time Impact, and Subordinated Market Observables
abstract: We consider two canonical market-microstructure regularities: the long-memory of trade signs and the square-root law of meta-order impact. The point is not to propose new empirical laws, but to separate the clocks on which existing laws are defined. The sign-memory law is an event-time statement about the ordering and fragmentation of hidden orders. The square-root impact law is an operational-time statement about front motion in a locally linear latent order book. Starting from a discrete-time random-walk bid/ask reaction--diffusion order book with a separate event clock, we identify an event-time imbalance reduction, derive the operational-time front and impact equations in the locally linear regime, and then subordinate both sign and impact observables to calendar time. Fractional or tempered clock effects enter through this event-to-calendar projection, not through a different operational-time impact mechanism. This gives a compact clock-aware framework in which event-time sign persistence, operational-time square-root impact, and anomalous calendar-time effects appear as distinct but compatible consequences of a common order-book representation.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive framework to analyze market microstructure by distinguishing between event-time, operational-time, and calendar-time dynamics. It shows that observed memory and impact laws are fundamentally defined on different 'clocks,' with calendar-time anomalies arising only from the projection of the underlying physics.
main_problem: The paper aims to rigorously separate the distinct time scales (clocks) governing two key market microstructure regularities: the long-memory of trade signs and the square-root law of meta-order impact.
main_result: It establishes a clock-aware framework showing that the sign memory is an event-time phenomenon, the impact law is operational-time, and anomalous calendar-time effects arise purely from the subordination (projection) of these underlying dynamics.
method: The authors model the system using a discrete-time random-walk bid/ask reaction-diffusion order book, deriving continuum limits and then explicitly subordinating the event-time and operational-time observables to calendar time.
model_or_system: The model is a discrete-time random-walk bid/ask reaction-diffusion order book, analyzed through its latent order book representation. The dynamics are separated into event-time (order flow signs) and operational-time (front motion/impact).
key_observables: Event-time imbalance field ($\phi_m$), trade sign autocorrelation ($C_	au(\epsilon)$), operational-time front position ($y(u)$), and subordinated calendar-time impact ($p(t)$).
important_parameters: The separation hinges on the nature of the waiting-time process (e.g., finite mean vs. heavy-tailed waiting times $ eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the locally linear, frozen-background latent-order-book approximation and the assumption that the underlying dynamics are separable across the three time clocks.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the hierarchy of time scales: event time (lowest layer, order-flow signs), operational time (middle layer, $\sqrt{u}$ front evolution), and calendar time (upper layer, subordinated impact process).
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining the system on an event clock, deriving the operational-time continuum limit and the impact law, and finally introducing the subordination mechanism to map these results onto the observed calendar time.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the methodology of separating underlying physical processes (event-time vs. operational-time) from the measurement/sampling process (calendar-time subordination) is a powerful, general technique applicable to non-equilibrium statistical physics and open quantum systems.
